questions.stem: Which statement describes the nuclear model of the atom?
options: A tiny, dense, positive nucleus surrounded by electrons in mostly empty space
A sphere of positive charge with electrons spread evenly through it
A large, positive nucleus filling most of the atom, with electrons on its surface
A cloud of protons and neutrons with electrons in a dense central core
questions.explanation: In the nuclear model the nucleus holds almost all of the atom's mass and all of its positive charge in a tiny central region, with electrons around it and the atom mostly empty space. A sphere of positive charge with embedded electrons was the earlier plum pudding model.

questions.stem: How many neutrons are in a nucleus of the nuclide ²³⁹₉₄Pu?
questions.explanation: The upper number is the mass number A (protons plus neutrons) and the lower number is the atomic number Z (protons). Neutrons = A − Z = 239 − 94 = 145. Adding the two numbers gives 333, which has no meaning.

questions.stem: Why do the protons in a nucleus repel each other?
options: The strong nuclear force between protons is repulsive at every distance
The neutrons between them push the protons apart to keep the nucleus stable
They all carry positive charge, so the electrostatic force between them is repulsive
They spin in opposite directions, so the magnetic forces between them push them apart
questions.explanation: Like charges repel, so every proton repels every other proton through the electrostatic (Coulomb) force. The strong nuclear force is attractive at the distances between neighbouring nucleons, which is why nuclei can exist at all.

questions.stem: What holds the protons and neutrons of a nucleus together despite the repulsion between the protons?
options: The strong nuclear force, which attracts nucleons over very short distances
The gravitational force, which is very strong inside the tiny nucleus
The electrostatic force between the protons and the orbiting electrons
The strong nuclear force, which attracts nucleons over very large distances
questions.explanation: The strong nuclear force acts between all nucleons, protons and neutrons alike, and is attractive and stronger than the electrostatic repulsion at distances of about the size of a nucleus. Its range is very short, so it has almost no effect beyond neighbouring nucleons. Gravity is far too weak to matter in a nucleus.

questions.stem: In a large nucleus, how do the forces on one proton at the edge compare?
options: It is attracted by every other nucleon but repelled only by its nearest protons
It is repelled by every neutron but attracted by every other proton in the nucleus
It feels no electrostatic force because the neutrons shield it from the protons
It is repelled by every other proton but attracted only by its nearest nucleons
questions.explanation: The electrostatic force has a long range, so a proton is repelled by all the other protons in the nucleus. The strong force acts only over very short distances, so only nearby nucleons attract it. As nuclei grow, repulsion catches up with attraction, which is why very large nuclei are unstable.

questions.stem: Why does a stable nucleus need a balance of neutrons and protons, with more neutrons in heavier nuclei?
options: Neutrons carry negative charge that cancels the charge of the protons
Neutrons are lighter than protons, so they reduce the mass of the nucleus
Neutrons repel the protons, keeping them far enough apart to be stable
Neutrons add strong-force attraction without adding electrostatic repulsion
questions.explanation: Each neutron attracts its neighbours by the strong force but is uncharged, so it adds no repulsion. Heavier nuclei have more protons repelling each other, so they need proportionally more neutrons to stay stable. Neutrons have no charge and are slightly heavier than protons.

questions.stem: What is natural radioactive decay?
options: A stable nucleus emits radiation after it absorbs a neutron from outside
An atom gives off light when its electrons fall to lower energy levels
A nucleus splits into two halves when it is struck by another nucleus
An unstable nucleus spontaneously emits radiation to become more stable
questions.explanation: Radioactive decay is spontaneous: an unstable nucleus emits alpha, beta or gamma radiation, without any outside cause, and becomes more stable. Splitting a nucleus by bombarding it is induced fission, and light from electron transitions is not nuclear at all.

questions.stem: Which correctly gives the charges of an alpha particle, a beta-minus particle and a gamma ray?
questions.explanation: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus with two protons, so its charge is +2. A beta-minus particle is an electron, charge −1. A gamma ray is electromagnetic radiation with no charge and no mass.

questions.stem: What is a beta-plus (β⁺) particle?
options: A helium nucleus emitted from the nucleus
A positron emitted from the nucleus
An electron emitted from the nucleus
A proton emitted from the nucleus
questions.explanation: A β⁺ particle is a positron, the antiparticle of the electron, with the same mass but a charge of +1. It is created in the nucleus when a proton changes into a neutron. A β⁻ particle is an electron.

questions.stem: Which ranks alpha, beta and gamma radiation from most to least ionising?
options: Beta, alpha, gamma
Alpha, gamma, beta
Alpha, beta, gamma
Gamma, beta, alpha
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are massive and doubly charged, so they ionise strongly and lose energy quickly, which is why paper stops them. Gamma rays are uncharged and ionise weakly, so they are the most penetrating. Penetrating ability ranks in the reverse order to ionising ability.

questions.stem: A source's count rate is 900 counts per minute with nothing in the way, 410 with paper in front, 32 with 3 mm of aluminium, and 31 with 1 cm of lead. Background is 30 counts per minute. What does the source emit?
options: Alpha and beta radiation but no gamma
Beta and gamma radiation but no alpha
Alpha and gamma radiation but no beta
Gamma radiation only, at two energies
questions.explanation: Paper cuts the count sharply, so alpha is present. Aluminium cuts it to background, so beta was present and there is no gamma, which would pass through 3 mm of aluminium. Lead makes no further difference, confirming no gamma.

questions.stem: A nuclide has too many neutrons for its number of protons. Which decay is it most likely to undergo, and what happens in the nucleus?
options: β⁻ decay, as a neutron changes into a proton
β⁺ decay, as a neutron changes into a proton
β⁻ decay, as a proton changes into a neutron
β⁺ decay, as a proton changes into a neutron
questions.explanation: In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino. This lowers the neutron number by one and raises the proton number by one, moving the nuclide towards stability. β⁺ decay changes a proton into a neutron, which suits nuclides with too many protons.

questions.stem: A light nuclide has too many protons for its number of neutrons. Which decay is it most likely to undergo?
options: β⁻ decay, emitting an electron and an antineutrino
Alpha decay, emitting a helium nucleus
Gamma decay, emitting a high-energy photon
β⁺ decay, emitting a positron and a neutrino
questions.explanation: In β⁺ decay a proton becomes a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino, so Z falls by one and N rises by one. β⁻ decay would add a proton, making the imbalance worse.

questions.stem: Very heavy nuclides such as uranium-238 often decay by alpha emission. Why?
options: Alpha emission turns excess neutrons into protons without changing the mass
Alpha emission releases excess energy without changing the number of nucleons
Alpha emission adds two protons, which increases the strong force holding it
Alpha emission removes mass and charge, reducing the nucleus's size and repulsion
questions.explanation: An alpha particle carries away two protons and two neutrons, so A falls by 4 and Z by 2. This shrinks a nucleus that is too large for the short-range strong force to hold securely. Turning neutrons into protons is β⁻ decay, and releasing energy alone is gamma emission.

questions.stem: Polonium-210 (Z = 84) decays by alpha emission. What is the daughter nuclide?
options: ²⁰⁸₈₃Bi
²⁰⁶₈₂Pb
²⁰⁶₈₆Rn
²¹⁰₈₂Pb
questions.explanation: ²¹⁰₈₄Po → ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb + ⁴₂He. The mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number by 2, and Z = 82 is lead. Adding 2 to Z instead gives Rn, an error in the direction of the charge change.

questions.stem: Strontium-90 (Z = 38) decays by β⁻ emission. What is the daughter nuclide?
options: ⁸⁹₃₈Sr
⁹⁰₃₉Y
⁹⁰₃₇Rb
⁸⁶₃₆Kr
questions.explanation: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁹⁰₃₉Y + ⁰₋₁e + antineutrino. A neutron becomes a proton, so Z rises by one to 39 (yttrium) and A stays at 90. Lowering Z by one would describe β⁺ decay.

questions.stem: Sodium-22 (Z = 11) decays by β⁺ emission. What is the daughter nuclide?
options: ²¹₁₁Na
¹⁸₉F
²²₁₀Ne
²²₁₂Mg
questions.explanation: ²²₁₁Na → ²²₁₀Ne + ⁰₊₁e + neutrino. A proton becomes a neutron, so Z falls by one to 10 (neon) and the mass number stays at 22. Raising Z by one would describe β⁻ decay.

questions.stem: Technetium-99m, used in medical imaging, emits gamma radiation to become technetium-99. What changes in the nucleus?
options: Its mass number falls by 4 and its atomic number falls by 2
Its atomic number rises by one while its mass number stays the same
Its mass number falls by one as a neutron is emitted with the gamma ray
Only its energy decreases; its mass number and atomic number stay the same
questions.explanation: Gamma emission carries away energy from a nucleus in an excited state, leaving the same nuclide in a lower energy state, so A and Z are unchanged. The 'm' stands for metastable. A fall in A by 4 and Z by 2 is alpha decay.

questions.stem: Thorium-232 (Z = 90) decays through a series of alpha and β⁻ decays to stable lead-208 (Z = 82). How many of each decay occur?
options: 8 alpha and 4 β⁻
6 alpha and 4 β⁻
6 alpha and 2 β⁻
4 alpha and 6 β⁻
questions.explanation: Only alpha decay changes A: (232 − 208)/4 = 6 alpha decays, which lower Z by 12 to 78. Each β⁻ decay raises Z by one, so 4 are needed to reach 82. Forgetting that each β⁻ decay raises Z by one leads to the wrong number of beta decays.

questions.stem: In the reaction ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + x ¹₀n, what is x?
questions.explanation: Mass number on the left is 235 + 1 = 236. On the right, 141 + 92 = 233, so 3 neutrons are needed. The atomic numbers already balance: 92 = 56 + 36.

questions.stem: What is the half-life of a radioisotope?
options: The time for each nucleus to lose half of its protons and neutrons
The time for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay
Half of the time it takes for every nucleus in a sample to decay
The time for a sample's mass to fall to half of its starting value
questions.explanation: The half-life is the time for half of the undecayed nuclei to decay, so the activity also halves. Every nucleus decays completely, not by halves, and the sample's mass barely changes because the daughter nuclei stay behind.

questions.stem: A sample contains 6.4 × 10¹⁰ nuclei of an isotope with a half-life of 5.0 days. How many undecayed nuclei remain after 20 days?
questions.explanation: 20 days is n = 4 half-lives, so N = N₀(1/2)ⁿ = 6.4 × 10¹⁰ × 1/16 = 4.0 × 10⁹. Dividing by 4 instead of 2⁴ gives 1.6 × 10¹⁰, and 6.0 × 10¹⁰ is the number that have decayed.

questions.stem: A sample's count rate, corrected for background, is 480 counts per second. Three hours later it is 120 counts per second. What is the half-life?
options: 6.0 hours
1.5 hours
3.0 hours
0.75 hours
questions.explanation: 480 → 240 → 120 is two halvings, so two half-lives took 3.0 hours and each is 1.5 hours. Treating the drop to a quarter as one half-life gives 3.0 hours.

questions.stem: A detector records 530 counts per minute near a source, with a background of 30 counts per minute. What will the detector record after two half-lives?
options: 133 counts per minute
265 counts per minute
155 counts per minute
125 counts per minute
questions.explanation: The source alone gives 530 − 30 = 500 counts per minute. After two half-lives this falls to 500/4 = 125, and the background of 30 is still there, so the reading is 155. Quartering the raw 530 gives about 133.

questions.stem: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. A wooden artefact has one-eighth of the carbon-14 found in living wood. About how old is it?
options: 4.6 × 10⁴ years
1.1 × 10⁴ years
7.2 × 10² years
1.7 × 10⁴ years
questions.explanation: One-eighth is (1/2)³, so three half-lives have passed: 3 × 5730 = 17 190 years, about 1.7 × 10⁴ years. Multiplying by 8 gives 4.6 × 10⁴ years. Radiometric dating relies on the predictable rate of decay.

questions.stem: An alpha particle has a kinetic energy of 4.8 MeV. What is this in joules? Use 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
questions.explanation: 4.8 MeV = 4.8 × 10⁶ eV, and 4.8 × 10⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 7.7 × 10⁻¹³ J. Forgetting the 'mega' gives 7.7 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and dividing by the conversion factor gives about 3.0 × 10²⁵ J.

questions.stem: What is artificial transmutation?
options: Changing one element into another by bombarding its nuclei with particles
Changing one element into another by heating it to a very high temperature
The spontaneous decay of an unstable nucleus into a more stable nucleus
Changing an element into a different isotope by removing its electrons
questions.explanation: In artificial transmutation, a nucleus is struck by a particle such as an alpha particle, proton or neutron, and turns into a different nuclide. Natural radioactive decay is spontaneous and needs no incoming particle. Chemical changes such as heating or removing electrons cannot change an element.

questions.stem: Irène Joliot-Curie and Frédéric Joliot bombarded aluminium with alpha particles: ²⁷₁₃Al + ⁴₂He → ³⁰₁₅P + X. What is X?
options: A neutron
A proton
An electron
A positron
questions.explanation: Mass number: 27 + 4 = 31, so X has A = 1. Atomic number: 13 + 2 = 15, so X has Z = 0. A particle with A = 1 and Z = 0 is a neutron. The phosphorus-30 produced was radioactive, the first artificially made radioisotope.

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes artificial transmutation from natural radioactive decay?
options: Transmutation needs an incoming particle to strike the nucleus, while decay is spontaneous
Transmutation happens spontaneously, while decay needs a particle to strike the nucleus
Transmutation only changes the nucleus's energy, while decay changes the element
Transmutation only happens in stars, while decay only happens in laboratories
questions.explanation: Natural decay happens without any outside cause, at a rate set by the half-life. Artificial transmutation is triggered by bombarding a nucleus with a particle, as in Rutherford's transmutation of nitrogen into oxygen. Both change one nuclide into another.

questions.stem: What happens in the neutron-induced fission of uranium-235?
options: The nucleus emits an alpha particle after absorbing a neutron, releasing energy
The nucleus absorbs a neutron and becomes stable, absorbing energy in the process
The nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing neutrons and energy
Two uranium nuclei join to form one heavier nucleus, releasing neutrons and energy
questions.explanation: A uranium-235 nucleus captures a slow neutron, becomes unstable uranium-236 and splits into two medium-sized fission fragments, releasing two or three neutrons and a large amount of energy. Joining nuclei together is fusion.

questions.stem: In a nuclear reactor, each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons. For the chain reaction to run at a steady rate, on average how many neutrons from each fission must cause another fission?
options: All of them
About 2.5
Exactly one
Exactly two
questions.explanation: If exactly one neutron per fission goes on to cause another fission, the rate stays constant. If more than one does, the reaction grows rapidly; if fewer, it dies out. The extra neutrons are absorbed or escape.

questions.stem: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found barium after bombarding uranium with neutrons. What did Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch conclude?
options: The uranium nucleus had joined with a neutron to make barium
The barium had come from alpha decay of the uranium
The neutrons had turned into barium nuclei on impact
The uranium nucleus had split into two smaller nuclei
questions.explanation: Barium (Z = 56) is far lighter than uranium (Z = 92), so it could not be made by a small change such as alpha or beta decay. Meitner and Frisch explained that the nucleus had split roughly in half and named the process fission. Hahn received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery.

questions.stem: What is nuclear fusion?
options: A heavy nucleus splitting into two lighter nuclei
A nucleus capturing an electron from its own atom
A neutron changing into a proton inside a nucleus
Two light nuclei joining to form a heavier nucleus
questions.explanation: In fusion, light nuclei such as hydrogen isotopes join to form a heavier nucleus, for example ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n, releasing energy. Splitting a heavy nucleus is fission.

questions.stem: Scientists once thought the Sun's energy came from slow gravitational contraction. What is now known to be the source?
options: Radioactive decay of heavy elements at its surface
Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core
Nuclear fission of uranium spread through its interior
Chemical burning of hydrogen gas with oxygen
questions.explanation: Once nuclear reactions were understood, it became clear that stars release energy by fusing hydrogen into helium in their hot, dense cores. Gravitational contraction could not have powered the Sun for the billions of years shown by the age of Earth's rocks.

questions.stem: What is the mass defect of a nucleus?
options: The mass lost by a nucleus each time it emits a gamma ray during decay
The difference between the nucleus's mass number and its atomic number
The difference between the mass of its separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus
The mass of the electrons that must be removed before the nucleus is measured
questions.explanation: A nucleus has less mass than its protons and neutrons would have separately. This mass defect is equivalent, by ΔE = Δmc², to the binding energy: the energy needed to pull the nucleus apart into separate nucleons.

questions.stem: A nucleus has a mass defect of 3.0 × 10⁻²⁹ kg. What is its binding energy? Use c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: ΔE = Δmc² = 3.0 × 10⁻²⁹ × (3.0 × 10⁸)² = 2.7 × 10⁻¹² J. Forgetting to square c gives 9.0 × 10⁻²¹ J.

questions.stem: In a deuterium-tritium fusion reaction, the products have 3.13 × 10⁻²⁹ kg less mass than the reactants. How much energy, in MeV, is released? Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
options: 2.82 MeV
17.6 MeV
questions.explanation: ΔE = Δmc² = 3.13 × 10⁻²⁹ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 2.82 × 10⁻¹² J. Dividing by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per eV gives 1.76 × 10⁷ eV, which is 17.6 MeV. Forgetting the 'mega' leaves 1.76 × 10⁷, and not squaring c gives 5.87 × 10⁻⁸ MeV.

questions.stem: The binding energies of three nuclides are helium-4: 28.3 MeV, iron-56: 492 MeV and uranium-238: 1802 MeV. Which nuclide is the most stable?
options: Iron-56, which has the greatest binding energy per nucleon
Uranium-238, which has the greatest total binding energy
Helium-4, which has the smallest total binding energy
Uranium-238, which has the most neutrons per proton
questions.explanation: Stability depends on binding energy per nucleon: helium-4 has 28.3/4 ≈ 7.1 MeV, iron-56 has 492/56 ≈ 8.8 MeV and uranium-238 has 1802/238 ≈ 7.6 MeV. Iron-56 holds its nucleons most tightly. Total binding energy is large for uranium only because it has so many nucleons.

questions.stem: Per nucleon of fuel, nuclear fusion releases more energy than nuclear fission. Why?
options: Fission releases neutrons that carry away most of the energy it produces
A greater percentage of the reactants' mass is transformed into energy
Fusion reactions involve heavier nuclei, which contain more total mass
Fusion converts all of the reactants' mass into energy, but fission does not
questions.explanation: Energy released comes from the mass lost, ΔE = Δmc². Fusing light nuclei produces a large jump in binding energy per nucleon, so a larger fraction of the mass, about 0.4% for deuterium-tritium fusion against about 0.1% for uranium fission, becomes energy. Neither process converts all of the mass.
